High-Resolution European Soil Property Maps Based on LUCAS and AlphaEarth Satellite Embeddings

Researchers produced 10-meter resolution soil property maps for all of Europe (EU-27 + UK) using machine learning trained on LUCAS soil datasets with AlphaEarth Foundations satellite embeddings, covering soil texture, pH, bulk density, and coarse fragments — a significant leap from the previous 30–250m resolution.

Key takeaways
  • 10 m resolution soil property maps produced for EU-27 + UK, covering clay, silt, sand content, coarse fragments, pH, and bulk density
  • Previous European soil maps ranged from 250 m to 30 m resolution depending on the property; this work closes the resolution gap
  • Machine learning workflow trained on LUCAS soil datasets using AlphaEarth Foundations satellite embeddings as predictors
  • Artificial Neural Networks outperformed Random Forests, with R² values ranging from 0.21 (coarse fragments) to 0.69 (pH)
  • Uncertainty estimate maps were produced using Monte Carlo dropout
  • Maps support precision agriculture, soil health assessment at field scale, and spatial planning

World Maps Might Soon Get an Upgrade: The UN Votes to Endorse Equal Earth Projection

The UN General Assembly voted 164-1 to endorse equal-area maps like the Equal Earth projection over the 500-year-old Mercator, which drastically distorts Africa's true size — with only the United States voting against.

Key takeaways
  • The UN General Assembly passed a resolution on September 4 urging institutions to adopt maps that better represent countries' relative sizes, with 164 votes in favor and only the United States against
  • The resolution specifically recommends the Equal Earth projection, developed in 2018, as a fairer alternative to the 1569 Mercator projection
  • The #CorrectTheMap campaign, spearheaded by Togo and endorsed by the African Union, argues that the Mercator map diminishes Africa's significance
  • The resolution does not ban the Mercator map but urges governments, schools, and tech companies to use equal-area maps where relative landmass size matters
  • Togo will be the first country to update its geography textbooks, aiming to do so before the end of 2026

GPS Navigation and Traffic Concentration: When Everyone Follows the Same Route

A study published in Nature Communications by researchers from CNR-Isti and the University of Pisa shows that when too many drivers follow GPS navigation simultaneously, route diversity drops by up to 14%, concentrating traffic on the same roads and potentially reversing environmental benefits.

Key takeaways
  • A Nature Communications study by CNR-Isti and University of Pisa researchers simulated traffic in Florence, Milan, and Rome
  • The study integrated GPS data, road network characteristics, and routes from Google Maps, TomTom, Bing Maps, and Mapbox
  • Route diversity can decrease by up to 14% when all drivers follow navigation systems
  • A critical threshold exists between 60-80% of drivers using navigation, beyond which environmental benefits diminish
  • In some Rome scenarios, CO2 reduction benefits completely reversed at high navigation adoption rates
  • The problem is the gap between individual optimization and collective outcomes
  • Researchers call for algorithms that consider overall city-level effects, not just individual route optimization

There Is No Such Thing as a "UN Map With Borders": Guterres

  • The controversial map was created by UN Geospatial during the consultation process for the "Correct the Map" resolution, but Guterres called it "not an official UN map" — "the contribution of an NGO"
  • The map depicted Arunachal Pradesh and Aksai Chin without the Indian and Chinese "claim lines" that previous UN maps had used
  • India had voted in favor of the "Correct the Map" resolution but raised "anomalies" about the map with the UN

New World Map Makes Africa Look Bigger: What's the Fuss About? Cartographers Explain

Cartographers Jack Swab and Derek Alderman explain the UN's endorsement of the Equal Earth projection, why the Mercator map distorts Africa's true size, how the new projection works, and why the US was the lone "no" vote against the resolution.

Key takeaways
  • The UN passed a non-binding resolution endorsing the Equal Earth projection over the Mercator projection, which exaggerates land towards the poles by 2-14x
  • The Mercator projection remains useful for navigation (preserving compass bearings), which is why Google Maps and Apple Maps still use it
  • The Equal Earth projection minimizes distortions of continental sizes, making it better for educational, public communication, and policy purposes
  • Map-making is decentralized — no single authority regulates which projection is used; the UN endorsement is symbolic, not mandatory
  • The US was the only "no" vote, calling the resolution a "radical and ideological project" and objecting to language linking Mercator's distortions to colonial legacies
  • Ukraine raised concerns over the depiction of Crimea, while other nations raised contested territory issues — but these were geopolitical posturing, not map issues
  • African nations framed the resolution as "cognitive justice" — correcting the mental map that equates size with power and importance
2026-09-13 Jack Swab and Derek Alderman (The Conversation) Source article

Google Maps Is Now Terrible: Explained

The Drive explains why Google Maps and similar navigation apps have gotten worse at saving time: mass adoption of GPS routing means too many users are sent down the same alternate routes, creating a Nash equilibrium where individual optimization degrades collective outcomes — and there is no easy fix.

Key takeaways
  • An estimated 7 billion devices worldwide rely on GPS, from phones to golf balls
  • A 2019 study found that between 2007 and 2017, services like Google Maps saved 52 billion gallons of fuel and a trillion miles through more efficient routing
  • GPS adoption has generated an estimated $1.4 trillion in economic benefits since the 1980s
  • The core problem: routing apps don't track how many users they've sent on a given route and can't know where competitor services are sending users
  • When everyone uses the same app to avoid traffic, alternate routes become congested too, negating the benefit
  • This creates a Nash equilibrium where individual route optimization degrades collective traffic outcomes
  • There is no simple solution — the problem is structural to how decentralized routing works at scale

Mapping Silicate Minerals From Space

NASA-funded scientists have created the first global maps of silicate, sulfate, and carbonate minerals in Earth's arid regions using thermal infrared spectroscopy data from the ECOSTRESS and ASTER satellite sensors, enabling space-based identification of mineral resources including lithium-bearing rocks.

Key takeaways
  • Researchers created 1-kilometer resolution global maps of silicate, sulfate, and carbonate minerals using ECOSTRESS (ISS) and ASTER (Terra satellite) thermal infrared data
  • Thermal infrared spectroscopy is the only known method to detect silica from space, using each mineral's unique spectral signature
  • Silicate deposits are associated with lithium-bearing minerals used in batteries, making the maps valuable for resource exploration
  • Silicate alteration on the surface can also indicate underground geothermal activity, pointing to potential renewable energy sites
  • The maps were validated by comparing satellite observations with field data from sites in California, New Mexico, and Morocco
  • The data complement NASA's EMIT sensor, which detects oxides, sulfides, and clays associated with precious minerals
  • The dataset is publicly available through NASA's Earthdata Search and the Land Processes DAAC as GeoTIFF

Will the UN Decision Change Our World Maps?

The UN General Assembly adopted a resolution with 164 votes in favor and one against, calling for world maps to use representations that more faithfully reflect the relative size of continents — favoring the Equal Earth projection over the colonial-era Mercator projection.

Key takeaways
  • The resolution was passed with 164 votes for and 1 against, presented by a coalition of African countries led by Togo
  • The Equal Earth projection, developed in 2018, preserves proportional area while accepting distortions elsewhere
  • Greenland appears similar in size to Africa on Mercator maps, but Africa is actually 14 times larger
  • Brazil appears the same size as Alaska on Mercator but is in reality five times larger
  • UQAM geography professor Rodolphe Gonzalès frames this as a "symbolic injustice, a geometric injustice between North and South"
